title: Philosophy for women too
hookLine: Musonius Rufus argued women should study philosophy as men do (Musonius Rufus, Lecture 3)

lines: ROME, IN THE AGE OF EMPERORS.
SPINNING FOR HER, BOOKS FOR HIM.
cards: Rome, in the age of the emperors. A girl learns to spin wool, run a household, keep accounts, and marry well. Her brother, if the family has money, learns rhetoric and philosophy.
That's how things are usually done. Then a Stoic teacher stands up in front of his students and questions it. Not in a whisper: as a lecture, with arguments, one after another.
His name was Musonius Rufus, and one of his students is someone this path has quoted again and again. This week, the Stoics honestly, starting with him.

teach.b: Musonius Rufus was a Roman Stoic who taught in Greek, was banished by emperors who found him inconvenient, and taught a young man named Epictetus.
His lectures survive because a student wrote them down and a later collector, Stobaeus, preserved them. The third lecture asks whether women should study philosophy, and his answer is yes.
The arguments are simple and sharp.

teach.h: THE SAME REASON, THE SAME SENSES.
teach.b: Women have received from the gods the same power of reason as men. The same senses: sight, hearing, touch. The same natural desire for goodness, and they're just as pleased by fine and just actions.
So why should it be fitting for men to seek how to live well, and not for women?

In the next lecture he goes further: daughters should be educated the same way as sons, because the virtues, courage, justice, self-control, wisdom, are the same for everyone. Now the honesty this week promises.
Musonius still pictured most women running households, and he thought some tasks suit men and some suit women.

teach.h: NOT EVERYTHING, BUT THE MAIN THING.
teach.b: He wasn't arguing for everything people argue for today. But he did say the one thing that mattered most to a Stoic, virtue, belongs equally to both.
And women had a place in this family of schools long before him: Hipparchia, the Cynic philosopher, married Crates, dressed like him, argued in public and was remembered for it.
So in a school that says the only true good is character, the door to philosophy was, at least in principle, open to everyone with a mind. Philosophy for everyone.

how: People of many backgrounds read the Stoics today, and some point to Musonius Rufus's lectures as an early argument that philosophy belongs to all.

o: a Roman general who led armies against Carthage
the Roman emperor who wrote the Meditations in Greek
a Stoic teacher who argued women should study philosophy

s: Musonius argued women have the same reason as men
the same reason, senses and desire for goodness.
Musonius wanted exactly the equality we'd argue for today
he still pictured different tasks, but the same virtues for all.
we have Musonius's lectures because a student wrote them down

games.q: a Roman asks Musonius: should my daughter get the same education as my son?
o: yes, the virtues are the same for both.
games.why: in his fourth lecture he says daughters should be educated like sons, because courage, justice and wisdom are for all.

practice: Think of one idea from this path that has stayed with you: the jolt isn't me, draw the circles in, take a polite share, anything.

Think of one person you haven't shared it with, maybe someone nobody would expect to talk philosophy with, and picture telling them in plain words, over coffee. Let the idea sit in your mind, ready to hand over.

wordCard.voice: Musonius. The Roman Stoic teacher who argued women share the same reason and virtues as men, so philosophy belongs to them too.

orig.note: Greek: love of wisdom, from philos, loving, and sophia, wisdom.

carryVoice: Your line: philosophy for everyone. Same reason, same senses, same virtues. Day two hundred ninety-five, in the books.
